proof_summary: Assuming either family finite, bound its relevant primes by \(N\) and apply the decomposition hypothesis to \(n=(N+2)!/6\), obtaining \((N+2)!=p+q\) with \(p\) Sophie Germain and \(q\) the upper member of a twin pair. If the Sophie Germain primes are bounded then \(p\le N\), while if twin pairs are bounded then \(q\le N+2\); in either case the bounded summand divides \((N+2)!\) and is smaller than the other summand, forcing that other, supposedly prime summand to be composite.
